title: The Comet's Two Coats
spine: We follow a comet's portrait from the library to the August sky, solving why it sometimes wears a tail and why the sky sprinkles dust on the same night every year.

comet_name.role: The comet in the library book, which we nickname and track all story

wish_thing.role: The small silly thing Dad keeps wishing for on meteors

segments.text:
It is a summer afternoon, and we are at the library. Me, Dad, and my big sister, squeezed around one little table.

Dad is reading the newspaper upside down. He does not know it is upside down.

My sister is flipping through a big space book. Suddenly she stops. "Whoa," she says. "Look at this."

It is a comet. A lumpy, dirty snowball of ice and dust, zooming through space. The book says its real name is something long and boring, so we give it a better one. We call it {comet_name}.

"Here is the weird part," my sister says. She holds up two pages, side by side. "Look."

In the first picture, {comet_name} wears a long, glowing tail. It streams out behind it like a scarf in the wind. Beautiful.

In the second picture, there is no tail at all. Just the same lumpy snowball, dark and plain, like a dirty sock someone left in space.

"Same comet," my sister says. She taps one page, then the other. "Two coats."

Dad looks up from his upside-down newspaper. "Maybe it got cold," he says, "and took the fancy one off."

My sister rolls her eyes. But she is smiling. "Seriously, though," she says. "Why does it have a tail sometimes, and not other times?"

Nobody at the table knows. Not even Dad.

"Test one," my sister says. "Us. Right now."

So we raid the kitchen. Ice from the freezer, dirt from Dad's plant, cracker crumbs from the bottom of the box. We pack it all into one lumpy snowball. It looks exactly like {comet_name}. If {comet_name} were dinner.

"To the porch," my sister says. "The lamp can be the Sun."

Dad carries it on a plate like a fancy dessert. "I shall miss him," he says.

We set our comet under the porch lamp and we wait.

Then — wisps. Little curls of steam, lifting off the ice. The ice shrinks first. The dirt just sits there, exactly where we packed it.

"The tail," my sister breathes. "It's the ice! Warmed up, turning to gas. That's the glowing coat."

"And the crumbs stay behind," I say. "Like somebody snacking on the walk home."

Dad nods solemnly. "I knew it. I always snack on the walk home."

But my sister has gone quiet. She is looking at the library book again, at that one strange drawing. The one where the tail streams out ahead of the comet. In front of it.

"Our steam went up," she says slowly. "It didn't go backwards. And it definitely didn't go frontwards."

She taps the page. "So why does {comet_name}'s tail sometimes point the wrong way?"

Nobody knows. Not even Dad.

"Planetarium," my sister says. "They have a pretend comet. We can watch the whole trip."

The planetarium is dark and round and smells like old carpet. In the middle, on a long metal track, hangs a lump of dry ice. Above it, a lamp.

"That lamp," the planetarium lady says, "is the Sun. Watch close."

The comet starts to move. Slow. It loops way out to the far end of the track, into the cold dark corner. Nothing happens. No tail. Just a plain lumpy snowball, like a dirty sock someone left in space.

"Years," the lady says. "It spends years out there."

Then the comet swings back. Closer to the lamp. Closer. And — steam. A long glowing tail blooms off the ice, right on cue.

"There!" my sister grabs my arm. "That's the coat! It only grows near the Sun!"

"Ice, warming up," I say. "Leaving crumbs behind."

Dad is squinting at the ceiling. "I wish on that one," he whispers, pointing at a painted star, "for {wish_thing}."

"Dad. That's paint."

"A moth once," he says sadly.

But my sister is frowning at the model. The comet is heading home now, back toward the dark — and its tail is leaning away from the lamp. Still pointing away. Even on the return trip.

"Wait," she says. "If the tail is just melted ice, it should drag behind. But it doesn't. It points away from the Sun. Both ways."

She looks at me. "Why?"

Nobody knows. Not even the planetarium lady. Well — she knows. But she is smiling, and not telling.

That night we drive to a hilltop field. Me, Dad, and my sister, with a blanket and a thermos of cocoa. The ranger shows us where to spread out, away from the path. "Lie back," she says. "Eyes up."

"What did you find?" my sister whispers. I tell her about it. She nods, like she is filing it away.

Then the ranger tells us the secret. "Sunlight pushes," she says. "Like wind. So a comet's tail always streams away from the Sun." She holds up her hand, fingers spread. "When the comet is heading home, it chases its own tail."

Dad gasps. "Like a dog!"

"A very cold dog," my sister says.

"And the tail itself?" the ranger says. "Ice. Sun-warmed ice, turning to gas, blowing outward. The comet only grows its tail on the near part of the orbit. Close to the Sun." She smiles. "Two coats. One for near, one for far."

It clicks. Both mysteries, solved at once.

Then my sister opens her notebook. She goes quiet. "Look," she says. Her tally marks from last year. Circled. This exact week. "How did the sky know?"

We lie flat on the blanket. The grass pokes my back. I don't care.

"Shh," the ranger says. "Let your eyes learn the dark."

So we wait. We count slow minutes. One cocoa. Two cocoa. Three cocoa.

Then, little by little, the sky fills in. Stars I couldn't see before just pop into place, like somebody turning up a lamp.

"There!" Dad whispers. A streak. Quick as spilled salt.

"I wish," he says, very solemn, "for {wish_thing}."

The ranger chuckles. "You just wished on a grain of comet dust."

Dad sits up. "A crumb?"

"A crumb," she says. "{comet_name} drops them, circling the Sun, visit after visit. And Earth plows right through the trail. Same dusty road. Same week. Every year."

My sister grabs her notebook. "That's why my dates match!"

We count eleven streaks before the cocoa runs out. Eleven crumbs, falling home.

At the car, my sister circles next August in the notebook. I fold the blanket. It smells like grass. And in my pocket, wrapped in a tissue, is one little crumb of dirt from our test comet.

"For luck," Dad says.

Like we need it.

"Walk with me," the ranger says. So we do.

The field is dark and bumpy. Crickets everywhere. Dad keeps pointing. "There! No, there!"

"Watch where they start," the ranger says. "Not where they go."

We trace the streaks backward, with our fingers, like following string. And here's the strange thing. They all spray out of one spot. One patch of sky, between two stars.

"That's the radiant," the ranger says. "The crumbs all come from there."

"Crumbs?" Dad says.

"{comet_name} sheds dust on every trip around the Sun. A whole ribbon of it, floating in space. Earth's orbit crosses that ribbon in the same place, every single year." She taps my sister's notebook. "That's how your dates knew."

Dad stops walking. He spreads his arms. "Then I wish," he says, "for {wish_thing}!"

He trips over absolutely nothing. He wishes anyway, from the ground.

Back at the blanket, we split the last of the cocoa, three sips each. The ranger folds her star chart into my sister's hands. The shower's week is circled in red.

"Keep it," she says. "For next year."

Dad brushes grass off his knees. "Best wish I ever fell for."

gathered_but_unused: A comet is a dirty snowball made of ice, dust, and rock, and it only grows a tail when it travels close enough to the Sun for the ice to warm up and turn into gas.
A comet's tail always points away from the Sun, blown by sunlight and solar wind, so on the way back out the tail actually streams in front of the comet.
Comets travel in long, stretched-out orbits around the Sun, which is why some comets only visit our skies once every few dozen or hundred years.
A meteor is not a falling star at all. It is a tiny bit of space dust or rock, often no bigger than a grain of sand, burning up in a flash as it slams into our air.
A meteor shower happens when Earth, in its orbit, plows through a trail of dust left behind by a comet, so many bits burn up in the same night and seem to spray out of one spot in the sky.
Meteor showers return on about the same dates every year because Earth crosses the same comet dust trail at the same point in its orbit each time.
The best way to watch a meteor shower is lying on a blanket in a dark place, looking up with patience, because your eyes need time to adjust and the streaks come in surprises.
The dust trails that make meteor showers were shed by comets long ago, so when you watch one, you are watching pieces of a comet that may have passed near the Sun before you were born.
